chunks: Power supply efficiency: definition, measurement. The question: What is efficiency in a power supply? How can it be measured? Why is it important?
Efficiency is the share of the energy you take from a source that actually reaches the load. It is output power divided by input power.
Whatever does not reach the load is loss, and it all turns into heat. Efficiency tells you how warm the supply gets and how long a battery lasts.
Imagine pouring water from a jug into a leaky bucket. Whatever arrives in the bucket is the useful part, and the rest spills.
Efficiency is the ratio of what arrives to what you poured.
To measure it you have to measure both flows at the same time, and not just once, since the leak changes with how fast you pour.

At light load the fixed loss P 0 (30 milliwatts in this model) dominates, so efficiency collapses; the peak sits where fixed loss and quadratic loss are equal, at I equals square root of P 0 over R (the linear term lowers the peak but does not move it, because it costs the same fraction of power at every current); past the peak, I to the 2R erodes efficiency.
Model parameters are illustrative, not a specific part. Drag P₀ down to 5 milliwatts and the efficiency at 10 milliamps rises from 51% to above 80%.
Drag R up and the peak moves left and the full-load efficiency drops.
Efficiency: ( ): P out over P in , often given as a percentage. Power loss: P in minus P out , which becomes heat.
Electronic load: a bench instrument that draws a set current from the output. Load sweep: repeating the test at many load levels.
Four-wire sensing: measuring voltage with separate leads so the drop in the current-carrying leads does not count.
A supply gives 5 volts at 2 amps, so P out equals 10 watts. It takes 12 volts at 0. 926 amps, so P in about 11. 1 watts. Efficiency is 10 over 11.
1 equals 90 % , and the loss is about 1. 1 watts. If it were 70% efficient instead, the loss would be 4. 3 watts, nearly four times as much heat. That is the whole idea.
"Efficiency is output power over input power, so it's the fraction of source energy that reaches the load; the rest is loss and becomes heat.
I measure Vin, Iin, Vout and Iout together, with Kelvin sensing at the converter pins, an electronic load, and a warmed-up unit, and I sweep load and input voltage because efficiency is a curve.
It matters for heat, battery life, size and cost, reliability, and regulations."
